parts.title: A food supplement with many ingredients slows the loss of movement as worms age, and changes which genes are switched on in C. elegans
parts.abstract:
Abstract

When people try to slow ageing, the goal is not only to live longer. More importantly, it is to spend more of life in active good health, which scientists call healthspan. Changing what we eat has become a possible way to stay healthy as we age. Testing such changes in people would take several years and would need very large groups of people.

So we used C. elegans, a tiny roundworm that ages quickly, as a stand-in for studying ageing. We wanted to see how two food supplements that anyone can buy affect the way worms lose their ability to move as they age. We used movement as a sign of healthspan. Both supplements contain many ingredients: vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, amino acids and plant extracts. They also contain substances that are expected to help with ageing, such as dihydronicotinamide mononucleotide (a substance that boosts NAD+, a molecule that helps cells use energy), trans-resveratrol, taurine, pterostilbene and bioflavonoids. V14™ contains 40 or more ingredients, and AG1® contains 70 or more, plus 5 extra strains of probiotic bacteria.

We filmed the worms over time with a machine called WormGazer™ and tracked how they moved. Worms given V14™ moved more and faster as they aged, compared with worms given AG1® and with worms given only the liquid we used to dissolve the supplements.

To look for the reasons behind this, we measured which genes were switched on in worms given V14™. This showed changes in groups of genes that work together on the body's chemistry and on its defences against stress, both of which are linked to ageing. Taken together, our findings suggest that V14™ delays the loss of movement with age in C. elegans. They also point to the promise of carefully chosen food supplements for changing processes that matter for ageing in humans.

Keywords: Ageing, healthspan, Caenorhabditis elegans, dietary supplements, loss of movement with age, gene activity
parts.introduction_first: Over the past hundred years, people have come to live much longer on average. As a result, populations in richer countries are getting older. This brings more social and economic problems (Christensen et al. 2009; Osareme et al. 2024) and a higher risk of long-lasting illnesses (Niccoli and Partridge 2012). People define healthspan in many different ways (Masfiah et al 2025; Rattan 2026), but more and more researchers now want to extend the years spent in good health, not just the total number of years lived (Olshansky 2022; Osareme et al. 2024; Scott 2021). As a living thing ages, its body gradually works less well, and it becomes more likely to die. Scientists now know that ageing is shaped, at least partly, by genes and chemical processes that have been kept the same over the course of evolution. This gives us a starting point for designing treatments aimed at specific parts of ageing (López-Otín et al. 2013).
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions, limitations and future directions

Our study gives the first evidence that V14™, a food supplement with many ingredients, slows the loss of movement with age in C. elegans. It also changes which genes are switched on, and these changes can guide further research.

Our study does have some limitations. C. elegans is a well-tested and efficient animal for studying ageing processes that are shared across many living things. However, its body, the way it handles substances and its chemistry are different from ours, so our results cannot be applied directly to humans. V14™ needs to be tested at many different amounts to find the range that works best. Each ingredient needs to be tested on its own and in different combinations, to see how much each one adds to any slowing of the loss of movement. Even after that, the amounts and conditions we used in worms do not match how people would use the supplement. The changes in gene activity that we saw need more study, and they only show that the two things happened together. To show that these genes actually play a part in ageing, we would need experiments that change the genes themselves.

We also judged healthspan mainly by how well the worms moved, which is one important part of how well an ageing body works. Other tests could be added, such as how the worms respond to stress and how they behave. Even so, the effects we saw on movement, together with the gene changes linked to it, give supporting evidence that can help us come up with ideas to test in future studies. In conclusion, V14™ delays the loss of body function with age in C. elegans and affects biological processes that are shared across living things and are directly relevant to ageing in humans.
parts.introduction_rest:
Scientists have studied many small molecules as possible ways to slow ageing (Chin et al. 2014; Couteur and Barzilai 2022; Harrison et al. 2009; López-Otín et al. 2013). These include metformin, a medicine often used for diabetes, and rapamycin, a medicine that helps prevent the body from rejecting a transplanted organ. Others are α-ketoglutarate, and substances that the body can turn into NAD+, a molecule that helps cells use energy. Alongside medicines, people are also becoming more interested in food and diet as newer ways to support healthy ageing. Examples include polyphenols (natural plant chemicals), fatty acids and probiotics, which are helpful bacteria (Diwan and Sharma 2022; Gao et al. 2023; Pan et al. 2012; Wichansawakun and Buttar 2018; Pagliai et al. 2021). At the same time, the market for food supplements with many ingredients, aimed at health and a long life, has grown a great deal (Clausen and Schlueter 2017; MacGregor et al. 2021).

This is why it is so important to test such products carefully in living things before they are tried in people, so that any claims about how well they work are backed up by evidence. Tests in people are still the final standard. But they are very expensive and take a long time, and spotting a delay in ageing needs a lot of time. That makes them out of reach for almost everyone developing a new product. So we need stand-in animals that are cheap, give results that can be carried over to humans, and can be used early in testing to judge treatments meant to extend healthspan.

C. elegans is a tiny roundworm that lives freely in the wild. In the laboratory, it is kept on a diet of Escherichia coli, a common bacterium. It is a well-established animal for studying ageing (Lapierre and Hansen 2012; Markaki and Tavernarakis 2020). Scientists have many tools and resources for studying its genes. It is also a fast and cheap way to test whether a new substance or treatment affects healthspan or lifespan (Weinkove and Zavagno 2021). Recently, a machine called WormGazer™ has been used to film worms and track how their movement changes as they age. This gives a quick, automatic way to measure several signs of a worm's health as it ages (Jongsma et al. 2024; Zavagno et al. 2024). By watching how C. elegans moves from early to middle adulthood, we can quickly spot treatments that slow ageing, and at the same time see whether they harm health.

In this study, we used the WormGazer™ Automated Healthspan test, followed by a manual test of how long the worms lived, and a study of which genes were switched on. Together, these let us look at how V14™, a food supplement with many ingredients that anyone can buy, affects the health of C. elegans as it ages. We compared V14™ with AG1®, another food supplement with many ingredients that anyone can buy and take every day. Both contain vitamins, minerals, antioxidants, amino acids and plant extracts. Both also contain ingredients that are linked to the body's processes for ageing, such as substances that boost NAD+ and bioflavonoids. V14™ contains 40 or more active ingredients, and AG1® contains 70 or more, plus extra strains of probiotic bacteria (Tables 1 and 2). Each supplement is designed to act on processes in the body that are linked to better health in humans (V14 Longevity Reds, n.d.; What Is AG1?, n.d.).

Here, we present evidence that V14™ delays the loss of movement with age in C. elegans. This gives a strong reason, based on tests in living things, to study it further as a way of using food and diet to support healthy ageing. The changes in gene activity that we saw after giving V14™ open up interesting directions for future research.
parts.methods:
Methods

The worms we used and how we kept them

We got our bacteria and worms from the Caenorhabditis Genetics Center (CGC), a centre that supplies C. elegans to researchers. It is paid for by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH Office of Research Infrastructure Programs, grant P40OD010440). We used two strains, or types, of C. elegans. The first is N2, the standard wild-type strain, meaning the normal, unchanged worm. The second is SS104, which carries a change in a gene called glp-4 (written glp-4(bn2)). Worms with this change cannot have young at a certain temperature. We kept SS104 worms at 15 °C, a temperature at which they can live and reproduce.

We used SS104 worms in the WormGazer™ experiments and in the lifespan tests, at a temperature of 24 °C. At this temperature the worms cannot have young, so their offspring could not get in the way of our measurements (Zavagno et al. 2024). We kept both strains at the same temperature, so that conditions were consistent and the timing of our work was easier to manage.

Making the agar plates

We grew the worms on Petri dishes filled with a jelly called agar. The jelly was made from a recipe called defined media (DM). In the standard recipe for growing roundworms (Brenner 1974), a food called peptone is used. Peptone is a mix of protein pieces, and its exact make-up can vary from one batch to the next. To reduce this variation, we replaced the peptone with a set list of amino acids and trace metals, as described before (Virk et al. 2016). We also added vitamin B12 (Maynard et al. 2018).

The amounts of a supplement that work in worms cannot be compared directly with the amounts that work in people. This is because the supplement enters the body in different ways, and the body handles it differently. We were aware that V14™ and AG1® were given in different doses (15 g and 13 g respectively). So we designed our experiments to give the same final amount of each supplement in the worms: 1.56 mg/ml for V14™ and 1.25 mg/ml for AG1®.

Neither supplement dissolved well enough in water, so we dissolved them in DMSO, a liquid that dissolves many substances. Even in DMSO, some bits did not dissolve, so we had to spin the liquid very fast in a machine called a centrifuge to push these bits to the bottom. We first made a strong starting solution, 100 times stronger than the final amount we wanted. For V14™ this was 312.5 mg/ml, and for AG1® it was 250 mg/ml. We spun these starting solutions at 6000 rpm for 10 minutes to push the floating bits to the bottom. We then collected the clear liquid on top and spun it again at 15000 rpm for 10 minutes to remove any bits still floating. We collected this liquid and diluted it further with DMSO, giving stock solutions of 156 mg/ml for V14™ and 125 mg/ml for AG1®.

To make each test plate, we added 1.5 ml of the stock solution to 150 ml of agar. This gave the final amounts of 1.56 mg/ml for V14™ and 1.25 mg/ml for AG1®. For comparison plates, which had no supplement, we added 1.5 ml of DMSO to 150 ml of agar instead.

We poured the Petri dishes for filming with DM agar 3 days before adding the worms. The next day, we added 100 µL of E. coli OP50 bacteria that had been growing overnight. We kept the dishes at 20 °C with controlled humidity until 24 hours after adding the bacteria. Then we moved them to an incubator at 24 °C.

Checking that the supplements did not harm the worms' growth

We wanted to be sure that the supplements did not harm the worms, either by poisoning them quickly or by stopping them from growing and developing normally. To check this, we used a test called DoseFinder (Zavagno et al. 2024). We gave wild-type N2 worms each supplement at 5 mg/ml, 2.5 mg/ml and 1.25 mg/ml. We then added E. coli to these plates. After 24 hours, we looked at the plates to see how well the bacteria had grown and whether they had formed a continuous layer, called a bacterial lawn.

Next, we added four N2 worms at the L4 stage, the last young stage before adulthood, to each plate at 24 °C. On days 3 and 5, we looked at whether the worms had started to have young and how they were developing. These were the days when the second generation of worms appears. We also looked at how much of the bacterial lawn the worms had eaten, as another sign of how well they were growing and developing. The supplements had no effect on bacterial growth or on the worms' growth and development. This showed that the amounts we chose for the later tests, described above, were suitable.

Healthspan tests using WormGazer™

To prepare for the WormGazer™ experiments, we placed adult worms carrying eggs onto 9-cm Petri dishes 4 days before putting them on the machine, so they could lay their eggs. We removed the mothers after 48 hours. Then, 24 hours later, we moved the dishes to 24 °C. This made sure there would be plenty of L4 young worms (in the case of N2), and it stopped the SS104 glp-4(bn2) worms from having young. The next day, we picked 12 L4 young worms onto each 3.5-cm Petri dish. We then loaded the dishes into the machines and left them undisturbed for the whole experiment.

We watched the dishes continuously with WormGazer™, as described before (Zavagno et al. 2024). After filming for seven days, we checked each dish. If a dish failed this quality check, we left it out of our analysis. For example, we left out dishes where bacteria or fungi had grown, or where the worms had burrowed into the agar.

Lifespan tests by hand

As soon as the WormGazer™ experiment ended, we moved all the worms by hand onto new 6-cm dishes containing the same supplements, so we could follow how long they lived. We checked the dishes by hand until every worm had died. Every 48 hours, we gently poked the worms with a platinum pick to see whether they moved, and we marked them as dead if they did not. On days 7 and 14, we moved the worms onto new dishes without the supplements. We left out of the analysis any worms that had swollen up with eggs (bagged), had a burst vulva (the opening used to lay eggs) or had crawled off the dish.

We then used a computer program called GraphPad Prism to draw Kaplan–Meier curves. These are graphs that show what share of the worms are still alive at each age.

Measuring which genes are switched on

We gave worms V14™ on agar plates at 1.56 mg/ml, as described above, for either 3 or 6 days. We collected at least 60 worms for each repeat, and we did four repeats for each condition. We washed the worms well with M9 buffer, a salt solution, and kept them in a liquid that protects RNA until we were ready to use them. The company Novogene (UK) took the RNA out of the worms and read it. RNA is the working copy a cell makes from a gene when that gene is switched on, so reading it shows which genes are active.

We then used a tool called Panther (https://geneontology.org/) to look for groups of genes that work together that were switched on more often than expected. This is called a GO enrichment analysis.

How we analysed the numbers

For the WormGazer™ results, the shaded band around each curve shows how much the average might vary. It is one standard error of the mean, across the curves for each dish within a condition. A standard error is a measure of how precisely we know an average: the smaller it is, the more precise the average. The error bars on the bar charts show the same thing: one standard error of the mean, across the measurements for each dish within a condition.

When we compared two conditions on a bar chart, we worked out the difference between their averages. We then worked out the standard error of that difference, based on the standard error of each measurement, using a standard method for adding up uncertainty (Gaussian error statistics). We then judged whether the difference was statistically significant by comparing it with its standard error. A difference is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.

We marked a difference of less than 1.64 standard errors as not significant (ns). A difference between 1.64 and 2.33 standard errors got one star (*), which means p < 0.05 on a one-sided test. A difference between 2.33 and 2.83 standard errors got two stars (**), which means p < 0.01 on a one-sided test. A difference greater than 2.83 standard errors got three stars (***), which means p < 0.002 on a one-sided test. A one-sided test looks for a difference in one chosen direction only.

For the lifespan tests, we judged statistical significance using two standard tests, the Log Rank test and the Wilcoxon test, applied to the Kaplan–Meier survival curves.
parts.results:
Results

V14™ delays the loss of movement with age

We filmed the worms with WormGazer™ and measured several features of their movement. We ran the experiment twice, each time with a separate batch of worms. Scientists call these two repeats "biological repeats". In both repeats, worms given V14™ kept moving better as they aged, from day 3 to day 7, than worms given AG1® and worms given only the liquid we used to dissolve the supplements (the control). Worms given AG1®, on the other hand, moved less than the control worms.

To see this, we looked at the fraction of worms moving, which is the share of all the worms that were moving at a given moment. V14™ raised this share in late adulthood, from day 3.5 to day 5.5 (Fig. 1A). We did not see this effect in young adulthood, from day 0.5 to day 3.5. AG1® lowered the share of worms moving across the whole experiment, from day 0 to day 7.

We also worked out how many hours the worms spent moving. To do this, we added up the fraction of worms moving over time, a method called "area under the curve" (Fig. 1B). Worms given V14™ spent more hours moving in late adulthood (after day 3.5) than worms given AG1® or the control. This increase was statistically significant. A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference between the groups, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For p < 0.01, that means less than 1% of the time. AG1® lowered the hours moved compared with the control.

Fig. 1

Healthspan test of worms given 1.56 mg/ml V14™, 1.25 mg/ml AG1® or the DMSO control (the liquid used to dissolve the supplements), measured with WormGazer. A The fraction moving graph shows the share of worms moving during each filming window. The shaded band shows the standard error of the mean (SEM), a measure of how much the average might shift if we repeated the experiment. B Hours moved, found by adding up the fraction moving over time, for days 0–1, 1–3 and 3.5–7. n ≥ 108, 144 and 142 worms, 9–12 Petri dishes 3.5 cm across per condition. ** = p < 0.01, *** = p < 0.002, one-tailed test (a test that looks for a difference in one chosen direction).

We also looked at how fast the worms moved. Worms given V14™ moved faster than the control and AG1® worms very early on, before day 1, and again in late adulthood, after day 3.5. AG1® made the moving worms slower than the control (Fig. 2A). We saw a similar effect when we looked at the speed of all the worms, moving and not moving (Fig. 2B).

Adding up the worms' speed over time gives the distance they moved (Fig. 2C). In both biological repeats, worms given V14™ moved a statistically significant distance more than the control worms before day 1 and after day 3.5. AG1® caused a statistically significant drop in distance moved between day 1 and day 3.5 in both repeats. After day 3.5, however, the drop caused by AG1® was statistically significant in only one of the two experiments.

Fig. 2

Healthspan test of worms given 1.56 mg/ml V14™, 1.25 mg/ml AG1® or the DMSO control, measured with WormGazer. A The average speed of moving worms. B The average speed of all worms. C The distance moved, found by adding up speed over time, for days 0–1, 1–3, 4 and 3.5–7. n ≥ 108, 144 and 142 worms, 9–12 Petri dishes per condition. * = p < 0.05, *** = p < 0.002, one-tailed test.

V14™ and AG1® do not change how long the worms live

After the automatic healthspan test, we checked each worm's lifespan by hand. Across two experiments, neither V14™ nor AG1® had a repeatable effect on how long the worms lived (Fig. 3).

Fig. 3

Lifespan test of glp-4 mutant worms (a type of C. elegans with a changed gene) given 1.56 mg/ml V14™, 1.25 mg/ml AG1® or the DMSO control, measured with WormGazer™ and by hand after day 7. The survival curve shows the share of worms still alive at each time point. n ≥ 109, 131 and 144 worms, 5–6 Petri dishes 6 cm across per condition. ** = p < 0.01, *** = p < 0.002, one-tailed test.

V14™ changes which genes are switched on in C. elegans

We used a method called RNA-seq to measure which genes were switched on in worms given 1.56 mg/mL of V14™ for 3 days and for 6 days. RNA-seq reads the messages that cells make from their genes, so it shows which genes are active. The results showed a statistically significant change in gene activity at both time points (adjusted p < 0.05, Fig. 4). The "adjusted" p-value is corrected because we tested thousands of genes at once.

On day 3, 17 genes were turned down and 75 were turned up. By day 6, 17 genes were turned down and 131 were turned up. Some genes changed in the same direction at both time points: 2 were turned down and 37 were turned up (Fig. 4A).

Next, we asked whether the turned-up genes belonged to particular kinds of jobs more often than chance would predict. This is called a GO enrichment analysis, and we used a false discovery rate (FDR) below 0.05. The FDR is a stricter version of the p-value that allows for testing so many genes at once. For biological processes, the turned-up genes showed no statistically significant results at either time point. However, on day 3 and on day 6, the turned-up genes were enriched for several biological processes, as shown in Fig. 4B and C.

Fig. 4

Gene activity in glp-4 mutant worms given 1.56 mg/ml V14™ or the DMSO control for 3 or 6 days, measured with RNA-seq. A Venn diagrams showing the genes whose activity changed (FDR P < 0.05). B GO analysis of turned-up genes on day 3. C GO analysis of turned-up genes on day 6. The numbers in B and C are −log10(FDR), rounded to 3 decimal places. 4B and 4C were made with ShinyGO 0.80 (Ge et al. 2020).

Overall, V14™ mostly turned genes up at both time points. From day 3 to day 6, genes for breaking down foreign chemicals and for handling sphingolipids (a type of fat found in cell membranes) were turned up more and more. Genes for breaking down hydrogen sulfide and for the mitochondrial respiratory chain (the system inside cells that releases energy) were changed in the same direction at both time points. These changes were linked to a lighter load on the body's chemistry and to keeping the mitochondria, the cell's power stations, working well.

Notably, the gene activity did not change in several pathways linked to ageing. These include insulin/IGF-1 signalling, TOR, AMPK and autophagy, which are systems that control growth, energy use and the recycling of old cell parts. We still need targeted experiments that test what these genes do to find out why the worms moved better.
parts.discussion:
Discussion

More and more food supplements are no longer just meant to stop people from missing out on nutrients. They are also meant to tackle ageing and the diseases that come with it. So we need quick, efficient ways to test how these supplements work in experiments where we can watch ageing happen. In this study, we set out to see how V14™ affects the way C. elegans worms lose their ability to move as they age. V14™ contains a large number of ingredients. Each one is thought, but not yet shown, to help people live longer.

Movement is a complicated trait. It depends on many processes in the body working together, such as muscles and nerve cells coordinating with each other. That makes it an excellent sign of how healthy a worm is. Tracking how movement declines over time also gives us a measure of ageing that changes as it happens. Our idea was this: if any ingredient in V14™ protects worms from losing movement as they age, whether on its own or because ingredients work better together than each would alone, we should be able to detect it in C. elegans using the WormGazer™ machine. We also included a second product, AG1®, which also contains ingredients thought to be good for human health.

Earlier studies have already shown some effects of AG1®. In one study, scientists moved the bacteria that normally live in the human gut into a different animal and gave them AG1®. The supplement acted as a partner that helped these bacteria, and it led to a statistically significant rise in the total amount of short-chain fatty acids (small acids made when bacteria break down food), along with acetate, propionate and other substances the bacteria produce (Kirby et al. 2023). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. In another experiment, done in the lab rather than in living animals, AG1® might also help keep the gut wall from becoming leaky, possibly because it increases the production of short-chain fatty acids (Sapp et al. 2024). In a clinical trial in people, AG1® was given to some participants and a placebo (a dummy pill) to others. The trial was randomised, meaning chance decided who got which, and double-blind, meaning neither the participants nor the researchers knew who got what. AG1® increased the share of helpful bacteria in the gut, and it could improve how well people felt their digestion was working (La Monica et al. 2024).

AG1® has been suggested to bring several benefits. These include less tiredness and fatigue, better mental performance and thinking, and support for digestion and the immune system. However, it makes no claims about helping people live longer. V14™, on the other hand, was designed to help people live longer, because it is made of ingredients thought to target the main features of ageing. Tables 1 and 2 list the ingredients in both V14™ and AG1®, along with published, peer-reviewed studies that support ageing-related effects of each ingredient.

The two supplements share a core group of ingredients, but V14™ also contains a set of substances that AG1® does not have. One of these is NMNH, a substance that boosts NAD+. NMNH has been shown to slow down glycolysis, the process cells use to break down sugar for energy (Liu et al. 2021). This fits with the changes in the worms' body chemistry that we saw when we measured which genes were switched on. Another ingredient, trans-resveratrol, has been shown in clinical trials in people to lower total cholesterol by a statistically significant amount (Cao et al. 2022). It also plays a key part in controlling how the body handles fats and sugars (Zhou et al. 2022). In a formula with so many ingredients, it is hard to pin down exactly which one causes the improvements we saw. Still, it is plausible that NMNH, trans-resveratrol, or other ingredients in V14™ working together are behind these positive effects.

Studies in C. elegans have shown that living longer does not always mean spending more time in good health. Bansal et al. (2015) looked at four mutant strains of C. elegans that live longer than normal: daf-2(e1370), eat-2(ad1113), ife-2(ok306) and clk-1(qm30). These worms spent a larger share of their time in a frail state. In another study, researchers measured muscle strength as a sign of health in four more long-lived mutant strains: eat-2(ad1116), daf-2(e1370), daf-2(e1368) and glp-1(e2141). In these worms, healthspan was not shorter. Instead, it was stretched out over time, so the worms stayed healthy for longer (Statzer et al. 2022). A recent review concluded that when C. elegans lives longer because it eats less, it also spends more time in good health (Loo et al. 2023).

We do not yet know whether different amounts of V14™ could also affect how long the worms live. Even so, we still hold the idea that treatments which improve health in ageing people will have a big effect on quality of life, and may also help people live longer by delaying the start of age-related diseases (Kaeberlein et al. 2015; Milman and Barzilai 2023).

To look for possible reasons, we measured which genes were switched on in the worms, using a method called RNA sequencing. We then used a GO enrichment analysis. This checks whether the changed genes are linked to particular jobs in the cell more often than we would expect by chance. We looked at genes that were turned down on Day 3 and on Day 6. For these, the analysis found no statistically significant enrichment in any job (FDR P < 0.05). The FDR, or false discovery rate, is a stricter version of the usual test that allows for the fact that we checked many genes at once.

The genes that were turned up on Day 3 were different. They were enriched in jobs involved in breaking down sphingolipids, membrane lipids and glucosylceramide (Fig. 4B, C). Sphingolipids are complex fats that are common in the thin outer layer of cells, called the membrane. They affect the membrane's structure and how freely it flows. They also control many processes in the body, including how cells pass on signals, how cells specialise, how cells die in a planned way, and how cells clean up and recycle their own parts (Li et al. 2025). Glucosylceramides are one type of sphingolipid, and they have been shown to play a part in how long C. elegans lives. For example, a type called C22 glucosylceramide is essential for the longer life that the glp-1 gene gives worms. When worms are fed sugar, making less glucosylceramide makes their lives much shorter (Xatse and Olsen 2023).

On Day 6, the genes that were turned up were enriched in jobs involved in responding to stress, to living things around the worm, to partner organisms, to other organisms, and to the immune system. It is well known that these responses are closely linked to how long C. elegans lives. Two signalling systems in the worm, called the PMK-1 pathway and the DAF-2/DAF-16 pathway, control the immune system, and this control is a key factor in how long the worm lives (Troemel et al. 2006). Taken together, the changes in gene activity fit with a picture in which the worms step up the rebuilding of their fats early in adulthood (Day 3). They adjust the make-up of their membranes to keep their cells in balance. Later in adulthood (Day 6), they shift towards building up defences against stress and the immune system.

We will need more experiments to find out whether V14™ makes the worms break down more sphingolipids, and whether this in turn changes processes that delay the loss of movement. However, only a small number of genes changed on both Day 3 and Day 6. This suggests that C. elegans responds to V14™ differently at different ages. In fact, we cannot say whether these genes changed directly because of V14™, or whether they changed because the worms were in a more youthful state of body chemistry, as their movement data showed. More experiments will be needed to find out whether these results point to a shift in gene activity towards a slower state of ageing.

Taken together, our results show that giving C. elegans V14™ improves their movement, which is linked to spending more time in good health, without affecting how long they live. We can also suggest that this effect does not come from the worms getting more nutrients. Instead, it may come from changes in the worms' body chemistry in response to one or more of the ingredients in V14™.
